title: Pechtregon L’Antilope Morse Attachment System: 2026 Concours de Machines Winner – John Watson
content:
John and Cari were originally supposed to attend the 2026 Concours de Machines, but logistics proved to be too much. Luckily for them, the winner of the framebuilding challenge event, Matthieu Chollet‘s framebuilding brand Pechtregon, had his photographer, Laurent Belando, document his L’Antilope touring bike with a unique and cleverly designed Morse System. Read on for a rundown on the Morse bag attachment system, along with a brief on L’Antilope.

Concours de Machines: Background

The Concours de Machines is an annual event sponsored by the Association des Artisans du Cycle (the French Association of Bicycle Artisans), which revived the historic competition in a modern format starting in 2016 (originally initiated with help from Victoire Cycles and 200 Magazine).

For a thorough background on the event, we kindly request that you read Petor’s Reportage in our Archives: 2022 Concours de Machines.

One of the great things about the Concours is that the challenge changes from year to year. The Association des Artisans du Cycle presents a technical brief for framebuilders to build a bicycle that will adapt on the fly to meet a list of specific requirements. The bicycle is fabricated specifically to meet those challenges while riding a specified route. Post-event, a panel of judges rates how well the bicycle performed, met its standards, and was constructed.

This year, the brief asked for a lot from a single machine: stay quick on tarmac, make room for wider tires and the gear for a night outside, and shift between the two in under 20 minutes. In road mode, bikes could weigh no more than 8.8 kilograms and run tires no wider than 32 mm. In off-road mode, rubber had to measure at least 40 mm.

Then there was the accessibility requirement, which may be the most compelling part of the whole exercise. Working with the French Handisport Federation, the Concours asked builders to rethink how luggage is managed with one hand. This detail prompted some creative thinking about where a bag is grabbed, how it attaches, how it releases, and how it stays secure once it’s on.

For 2026, Pechtregon’s L’Antilope with the Morse Attachment System won the event. We’re lucky to have Matthieu Chollet from Pechtregon submit his winning bike to The Radavist.

Matthieu wrote a brief on the Morse System and L’Antilope below…

Pechtregon L’Antilope

I thought my bikes were simple and clever, but only for a cyclist with two hands. By putting yourself in another’s shoes, you see things differently.

We start to think differently, to not do what we are used to doing, to take one or more steps to the side. This approach allows us to evolve our human environment, the objects and services that surround us.

The Morse System

A simple answer to a gesture that has become complicated. Morse addresses the problem of attaching and detaching luggage with one hand. Initially designed to attach directly to a truss fork, it expands thanks to additional stainless steel supports that allow carrying capacity to be tripled.

The luggage module remains the same: it attaches to any of the bike’s six mounting points. A safety lock prevents the bag from flying up in the event of an impact.

Why “Morse”?

On a lathe or milling machine, the Morse taper allows a tool to be fitted in a single movement: the taper centers the workpiece and holds it in place with simple pressure. The Morse taper device applies this mechanical principle to the bicycle.

The plates are cut, perforated, and then anodized black: light, rigid, and engraved with Morse code.

Bag Attachment in Three Movements

Input
The bag is carried by its strap. The Morse module is attached to the back: it’s the same interface on all the bags.

Engage
The module is mounted on one of the six support points on the stainless steel fork or luggage rack. The bag is attached.

Roll
The safety lock secures the luggage in place during impacts. To remove it, reverse the action, always using one hand.

One Module; Six Slots

Truss fork at the front, additional stainless steel luggage racks at the rear: the same Morse module is used for both. The supports are also mounted and dismounted by hand, using knobs.

See more on the Morse System at Morse Equipment.

Pechtregon L’Antilope

A streamlined, sporty road bike weighing less than 8.8 kg, on which everything has been designed for speed and inclusivity: one-hand luggage, turn signals controlled from the handlebars on the left or right, wheels that can be replaced in one gesture, automatically connected lighting.

Legend Wheels Dual System

L’Antilope utilizes the Legend Wheels Dual system, which allows the rider to remove the wheel without faffing with the chain, derailleur, or cassette. Legend Wheels’ system revolutionizes the “one bike, two wheel setups” system: perfect for Concours de Machines.

Pechtregon L’Antilope Specs

  • < 8.8 kg: for a pilot of 188 cm
  • GRX 12s: mechanical single-chainring transmission
  • Legend Wheels Dual: rear wheel removal without touching the chain (see the video of it in action here)
  • SON SL: automatic electrical connection

Thanks to Matthieu Chollet for sending us this story and to Concours de Machines for hosting this wonderful event.
